title: Closing the Loop: Driving the Robot to a Target

questions.question: Why does the controller control heading rather than position directly?
options: A differential drive cannot move sideways, so commanding x and y asks for motion it cannot perform
Because position is harder to measure
Because heading errors are always smaller
Because a PID can only control one value
questions.explanation: The machine can turn to face a target and drive forward. Controlling heading and choosing a forward speed expresses exactly what it can do.

questions.question: How do you get wheel speeds from a forward speed and a turn rate?
options: Add and subtract half the turn rate times the wheel base from the forward speed
Multiply the forward speed by the turn rate
Divide the forward speed by the wheel base
Set one wheel to the forward speed and the other to the turn rate
questions.explanation: It is the model from lesson 00-04 rearranged. Forward is the average of the wheels and turn is their difference over the base, so going back is half the difference either side of the average.

questions.question: What happens if the heading error is not wrapped?
options: A target just behind produces an error of nearly a full turn, and the robot spins the long way round
The error becomes negative
The PID output saturates permanently
Nothing, atan2 already wraps its result
questions.explanation: atan2 returns a wrapped angle, but subtracting the robot's heading from it can leave the difference outside the range, so the difference has to be wrapped too.

questions.question: Why does the forward speed fade with aim rather than switching on and off?
options: A switch produces a step change in the command, which is what the rate limiter exists to prevent
Because fading is easier to compute
Because the PID cannot handle a step input
Because switching would exceed the wheel limit
questions.explanation: A step in the actuator command is exactly the lurch that lesson 14-02 was about. Fading keeps the behaviour continuous and the hardware happy.

questions.question: Why is the watchdog checked before any control arithmetic?
options: The safe state should not depend on the rest of the function being correct
Because the arithmetic is slow
Because the PID must not be updated twice
Because the watchdog needs the current time first
questions.explanation: Putting the stop first means a bug anywhere below it cannot prevent the robot from stopping. Safety checks belong at the top for that reason.

questions.question: A test that stops the moment the robot first arrives would miss which problem?
options: Overshooting, where the robot passes the target and has to come back
Turning the wrong way
Exceeding the wheel speed limit
Failing to move at all
questions.explanation: That is why the test keeps driving for several seconds after arrival and requires the robot to stay put. A follower that overshoots passes the naive version.
